1.pericope_label: My offering, my bread: the continual burnt offering

schools.summary: Gill counts the years: thirty-eight since these laws were first made, during which some fell into disuse, the generation that stood at Sinai being dead but for a few, while Moses was about to die and a successor had just been appointed. He adds the Targum's gloss that the morning lamb atoned for the sins of the night. Calvin presses the manner of the command. The verb rendered observe expresses not diligence only but obedience, and God stirs them to beware of transgression by calling the offering his bread, as if he ate as men eat. It is a hard expression, Calvin grants, but the rudeness of that people obliged him to speak so grossly, that they might learn the rite was as acceptable to God as food is to a man. He recommends the rite by its antiquity, since it began at Sinai, and notes that libations were in use among the heathen too, but without command or promise, and therefore unmeaning. Here, by contrast, men were reminded to have God before their eyes in their daily food.

Henry alone qualifies the premise that the sacrifices had lapsed. He will not grant that observance wholly ceased — the daily lamb, he thinks, was offered morning and evening and doubled on the sabbath — but that many sacrifices lapsed he takes as implied by the prophet's question, quoted afterwards by Stephen, whether they had offered him sacrifices those forty years. His own reasons for the repetition are that the new generation might be left without excuse, having the law now in less compass and a plainer method; that they were entering on war and might think that while the clash of arms lasted the law fell silent, whereas they were peculiarly concerned to keep peace with God while at war; and that in the wilderness an omission was less scandalous than it would be in Canaan among other peoples. On the daily offering he dwells: a lamb morning and evening, called continual for its constancy as duly as the day came, intimates that when we are bidden to pray always, at least every morning and evening we should offer our solemn prayers. Nothing is added in this repetition, he says, except that the wine of the drink offering is to be strong; and though it was poured out and not drunk, so that men might think the worst would serve to be thrown away, God requires the strongest, to teach us to serve him with the best we have. Ainsworth's reason, Henry adds, is that the wine figured the blood of Christ.

Wesley adds that the renewal was a testimony of grace notwithstanding how often they had forfeited it, though the chief reason was that they were ready to enter the land where these things must be practised. Clarke, admitting it is not easy to account for the precepts coming here, settles on two grounds: the services must now be constant in the land, and the former generation being dead, multitudes might be ignorant of them. He also sets out four ranks of offering, daily, weekly, monthly and annual.

Ellicott would render the phrase my oblation, even my bread, making the possessive the point: the offering, though presented by human hands, was God's and not theirs, since the silver is his and the gold is his. The word for bread may stand for food generally, the sacrifices being regarded as the Lord's food. He closes by reading the morning and evening lamb as a striking type of the Lamb of God offered once for all. Keil is more literal on the libation: in the sanctuary means round about the altar, as Josephus paraphrases it, not with holy vessels; and the word for strong drink means not intoxicating drink but strong drink as against water, the libation being wine only, which one paraphrase specifies as old wine.

debates.question: Had the sacrifices lapsed during the wilderness years?

positions.position: largely, yes — some fell into disuse across thirty-eight years, and a new generation had grown up ignorant of them
not wholly — the daily lamb continued and was doubled on the sabbath, though many other sacrifices were omitted

outliers.note: defends the harsh figure of God eating: the rudeness of the people obliged him to speak so grossly, that they might learn the rite was as acceptable to him as food is to a man

themes: why the sacrificial laws are repeated here
the continual burnt offering and its strong wine

9.pericope_label: The burnt offering of the sabbath, and of the new moons

schools.summary: Calvin puts the sabbath doubling as a supplement: what was omitted before is here supplied, that on the sabbath the continual sacrifice was doubled and two lambs offered instead of one, since it was reasonable that a day peculiarly dedicated to God should be exalted above the rest by some distinctive mark. On the monthly sacrifice he says the goat was added so that every month the people should present themselves as guilty before God to deprecate his wrath, the first day of each month being consecrated that they might more frequently have the remembrance of their duties renewed. Gill reports the rabbinic ruling on the phrase the sabbath in his sabbath: one sabbath's offering could not be brought on another, so that if the day passed and the offering had not been made, it lapsed and was not renewed, every sacrifice being due in its own season. He also infers the religious observance of the new moon from the trumpets, the resort to the prophets, and the abstinence from business.

Henry draws the practical inference from the doubling. Besides the two lambs of the daily burnt offering two more must be brought, one probably added to the morning sacrifice and the other to the evening, which teaches us to double our devotions on sabbath days. The rest itself he takes as a means rather than an end: it is observed in order to a closer application to the sabbath work, which ought to fill up sabbath time. On the phrase the sabbath in his sabbath he turns the words into a rule for the conscience: we must do every sabbath day's work in its day, redeeming every minute as those who believe it precious, and not put off one sabbath's work to another, since sufficient to every sabbath is the service thereof. He looks forward as well, taking the temple-service of Ezekiel's vision, where the sabbath offering rises to six lambs and a ram, to point at gospel times and intimate not merely the continuance but the advancement of sabbath sanctification under the Messiah. Of the new moons he observes that they and the sabbaths are often named together as great solemnities, comfortable to the saints and typical of gospel grace, and suggests that as the sabbath was kept with an eye to creation, so the new moons were sanctified with an eye to providence, which appoints the moon for seasons and guides time by her changes. Though we keep no feast of new moons, he says, we must not forget to give God the glory of all the precious things put forth by that faithful witness in heaven. Whether they ranked as feasts he thinks hardly doubtful, since besides the sacrifices the people rested from servile work, blew the trumpets, and went to the prophets to hear the word. On the sin offering he holds that when we give glory to God by confessing his mercies we must give it also by confessing our sins, and that when we rejoice in the gifts of providence we must make the sacrifice of Christ the fountain and spring-head of our joy. He ends with the figure the moon supplies: as she borrows her light from the sun and is renewed by its influences, so the church borrows hers from the Sun of righteousness.

Ellicott notes that the sabbath offering, added to the daily sacrifice, is enjoined here for the first time, the rule for its drink offering having been laid down earlier; and he adds that the new moon was announced by the blowing of the silver trumpets. Keil is careful on the standing of that day: the beginnings of months were distinguished by a festal sacrifice without being, strictly speaking, festal days with sabbatical rest and a holy meeting, though in later times the new moon grew more into a feast, trade being suspended and the pious seeking instruction from the prophets.

debates.question: Did the new moon rank as a feast?

positions.position: hardly doubtful — the people rested from servile work, blew the trumpets, and went to the prophets to hear the word
not strictly — it was distinguished by a festal sacrifice without sabbatical rest or a holy meeting, and grew into a feast only later

outliers.note: reports the rabbinic ruling that a missed sabbath offering simply lapsed and could not be made up the following week, every sacrifice being due in its own season

themes: the offerings of the new moons

15.pericope_label: The passover, and the seven days of unleavened bread

schools.summary: Gill pauses on the goat before the feasts. It was not a burnt offering but a sin offering, typical of Christ who was made an offering for sin; and it belonged, he says on Jewish authority, to that class of sin offerings which were eaten, since others, whose blood was carried into the sanctuary, were not. On the closing words he passes on Maimonides, who found the phrase unto the Lord very expressive, its design being to mark that the monthly sacrifice was made to the Lord and not to the moon, as the Egyptians did. The dating he explains as well: the fourteenth falls in the month which the exodus made the first, though otherwise the year had begun in autumn; and the fifteenth begins not the passover, which was the day before, but the seven days of unleavened bread, the first of which was kept very religiously. Calvin explains why he treats the passage under the head of the continual sacrifice. Since sacrifices are the avowed subject and no other observance is mentioned except in passing, he takes it as a concomitant of the daily offering: Moses refers cursorily to abstaining from leaven, then descends to his main point, that two bullocks, a ram and seven lambs, with a goat for a sin offering, should be slain, and the sacrifice repeated through the week. He finds three ends in that addition. It increased the reverence paid to the passover, so the people might be more stimulated to devote themselves to God; it made them acknowledge how familiarly he had embraced them with his favour, since he took these offerings from their own flocks and required the feast to be prepared out of their cellars and granaries too; and it made them profess themselves worthy of eternal death, so that they should fly to him for pardon and understand there was but one way of reconciliation.

Henry works the same material forward into the gospel. The first and last of the seven days were sanctified as sabbaths by holy rest and holy convocation, and on each they were to be liberal in their sacrifices, in token of a constant thankfulness for the deliverance out of Egypt; and a gospel conversation, in gratitude for Christ our passover, is itself called the keeping of this feast — for it is not enough to purge out the leaven of malice and wickedness, but we must offer the bread of our God, the sacrifice of praise, continually. At the day of the first-fruits a sheaf of barley had been brought at the earlier feast as an introduction to the harvest, and now, seven weeks later, a new meat offering at the end of it, in thankfulness to a God who had not only given but preserved the fruits of the earth; and it was at this feast, Henry notes, that the Spirit was poured out and thousands converted, presented to Christ as a kind of first-fruits of his creatures. When God sows plentifully upon us he expects to reap accordingly. Henry closes with Bishop Patrick's observation that no peace offerings are appointed in this chapter, those being chiefly for the offerers' benefit, who were left more to themselves; whereas burnt offerings were purely for the honour of God and confessions of his dominion, typifying that piety by which the soul is wholly offered up in the flames of holy love, and sin offerings were typical of Christ's sacrifice. No hurrying employments and no prosperous circumstances, he adds, should make us slack in these exercises.
Wesley identifies the feast in four words: namely, of unleavened bread.

Keil supplies the relation between the festal offerings and the daily: they were prepared in addition to the morning burnt offering, which served as the continual burnt offering — implying they were offered every day after it.

debates.question: Why was the ordinary sacrifice increased through the passover week?

positions.position: to increase reverence for the feast, to make them own God’s familiar favour, and to make them profess themselves worthy of death and fly to him for pardon
as a token of great and constant thankfulness for the deliverance out of Egypt

outliers.note: passes on Bishop Patrick's observation that no peace offerings are appointed in the chapter, those being for the offerers' benefit and left more to their own discretion

themes: the sin offering unto the LORD, not to the moon
the seven days of unleavened bread

22.pericope_label: The day of the firstfruits, and the numbers that do not agree

schools.summary: Gill will not let the sin offering pass as a formality. Notwithstanding all their services, and though the day itself was a holy convocation, there was still need of an offering to expiate their guilt — typical, he says, of Christ, who takes away the sins of our holy things as well as all our other sins. This goat too belonged to the class of sin offerings that were eaten, and he cites the rabbinic ruling that it was eaten on the second day of the passover. He notes that the evening sacrifice is meant as well as the morning, though not expressed, and that the same victims were brought on every one of the seven days, though they were not all holy convocations, only the first and the last. Calvin meets the numerical difficulty head on. The sacrifices for this day are here two bullocks and one ram, whereas Leviticus gives one bullock and two rams. Some think the choice was left to the priests, but when Calvin considers how precisely God's commands were given in everything, he questions whether such an alternative was left to anyone's discretion; and the notion that God had once been content with a single bullock because cattle were not abundant in the desert he calls a subterfuge. He confesses that he does not know how to get out of the difficulty, unless in this one respect the people were reminded that God in himself cares nothing for greater or smaller victims. Nor, he adds, does any reverence forbid us to say that a wrong number may have crept in through the carelessness of scribes, which he thinks probably the most natural solution; and the more correct reading, in his opinion, is two bullocks and one ram.

Wesley explains why only the morning sacrifice is named where both are meant. The celebration began with it, and that was the only one about which doubt could arise — whether it might be omitted when so many others were being offered that same morning — whereas nobody questioned the evening sacrifice, since at that hour there were no others to displace it. He also identifies the day of the first-fruits with the day the Spirit was given, and glosses the weeks as the seven numbered from the passover. Clarke gives the day its other names, the feast of weeks and pentecost.

Ellicott renders the Hebrew more exactly as in your weeks, at the expiration of a week of weeks from the morrow after the chief day of the passover. He states the divergence between this chapter and Leviticus without resolving it, and reports two ancient attempts: the Mishnah holds that the animals named in Leviticus were presented with the loaves, while those named here were additional sacrifices of the day, and Josephus reckons the whole at three bullocks, two rams and fourteen sheep. Keil adds the liturgical relation: the festal burnt offering and sin offering of that one day stood independent of the supplementary offerings that went with the wave-loaves, and were to be offered before those and after the daily morning sacrifice.

debates.question: How is the disagreement with Leviticus over the number of bullocks and rams to be resolved?

positions.position: probably a scribal error; the correct reading is two bullocks and one ram, and the appeal to priestly discretion or to desert scarcity is a subterfuge
the animals of Leviticus went with the wave-loaves, while those named here were additional sacrifices of the day

outliers.note: observes that peace offerings were also brought on this day though none are mentioned here, nor anywhere in the chapter

themes: the sin offering on a day of holy convocation
two bullocks and one ram, or one and two?

30.pericope_label: Beside the continual burnt offering: they shall be unto you without blemish

schools.summary: Gill observes that the closing clause ranges all these festal victims beside the continual burnt offering and its meat offering — that is, beside the lamb of the morning and the lamb of the evening, named so often through these verses and so frequently pressed as a thing never to be dropped, whether at the weekly, the monthly or the annual solemnity. He gives two grounds for that insistence: the rite was necessary in itself, and it was besides an eminent type of the great sacrifice of the Messiah. He construes the demand for what is without blemish as reaching to the drink offerings named alongside, so that the meal from which the accompanying cakes were made had to be clean and sound and untouched by vermin, while the wine poured out was not to be flat, spent or thick with lees. What such a standard came to in practice he illustrates from the rabbis, who reduced it to tests a treasurer could apply. Of the meal it was ruled that he should thrust his hand into the heap: if dust came away with it, the parcel was refused; if it bred worms, refused likewise — a judgment the commentators limit to the bulk of a quantity rather than a stray grain or two. Of the wine Jarchi reports that his teachers drew their rule from this very verse, holding any vintage unfit for libation in which flour rises, or a cloudiness resembling flour; and the warrant he pleads is the phrase before him, that what is brought should be perfect.

Clarke refuses to confine the demand that they be without blemish to the animals. It reaches, he says, not merely to beasts but to the flour, the wine and the oil alike: every thing must be perfect in its kind.

outliers.note: extends 'without blemish' beyond the victims to the flour, wine and oil, so that every thing must be perfect in its kind

themes: the rabbinic tests for meal and wine
